module_title: Computer Architecture - Machine Cycles, System Buses, and Specific Registers
introduction: This intermediate tier delves deeper into how the CPU actually executes a command. We explore the 4-step Machine Cycle, differentiate between the types of internal buses, and identify specific hardware registers like the PC and Accumulator.

core_concepts.title: The Machine Cycle (Instruction Cycle)
core_concepts.description: Every action performed by the CPU follows a strict 4-step cycle: 1. Fetch (retrieve instruction from memory), 2. Decode (CU translates the instruction), 3. Execute (ALU performs the math/logic), 4. Store (save the result back to memory/register).

core_concepts.title: Program Counter (PC)
core_concepts.description: A highly critical CPU register. It holds the memory address of the *next* instruction that needs to be fetched and executed. It keeps the CPU sequential and organized.

core_concepts.title: Accumulator
core_concepts.description: A specific register located within the ALU. Whenever the ALU performs a calculation, the intermediate and final mathematical results are temporarily stored in the Accumulator before being sent out.

core_concepts.title: System Bus Architecture
core_concepts.description:
A 'Bus' is a collection of wires through which data is transmitted. There are three main types: 
1. Data Bus: Carries the actual data.
2. Address Bus: Carries the location (address) of where data should go.
3. Control Bus: Carries the timing and command signals from the CU.

important_entities.name: Instruction Register (IR)
important_entities.significance: Unlike the Program Counter (which holds the *next* address), the IR holds the actual instruction that is currently being decoded and executed.

important_entities.name: Clock Speed
important_entities.significance: Measured in Hertz (Hz, MHz, GHz). It represents the number of internal cycles (pulses) the CPU can complete in one second. A 3.0 GHz processor completes 3 billion cycles per second.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The Fastest Memory Trap: Cache vs. Registers
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: This is the most confused question in computer static GK. If an exam asks 'Which is the fastest memory in a computer?', and 'Registers' is an option, it is the correct answer. Registers are fundamentally faster than Cache memory because they reside inside the CPU execution core.
Remember the directions: The Address Bus is 'Unidirectional' (flows only outwards from the CPU to memory). The Data Bus is 'Bidirectional' (data flows back and forth between CPU and memory).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this to remember the exact sequence of the Machine Cycle: Fetch -> Decode -> Execute -> Store.

exam_strategy_tips: Examiners frequently test the difference between the Program Counter (PC) and the Instruction Register (IR). Always map 'Next Address' to PC, and 'Current Instruction' to IR.
